sections.title: Objective type questions: each has two parts of 1 mark (match the columns, true/false, fill in the blanks or one-word answers).

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) Children's understanding about themselves, their feelings and how they sustain relationships with others are a part of their ________ development. (ii) Tying shoelaces is an example of the development of ________ motor skills.
questions.note: Part (i) was asked in April 2025 and part (ii) in April 2026.

questions.q: Fill in the blanks: (i) Pre-schoolers learn ________ skills necessary for interacting with other children. (ii) ________ refers to children's ability to identify similarities and differences in objects.

Match the development of six-to-eight-year-olds: (a) Language development (b) Cognitive development — (i) Can remember routes to familiar places (ii) Invent new words and phrases (iii) Grow about 1–3 inches a year
Match: (a) Physical development (b) Emotional development — (i) Verbalise conflicting emotions (ii) Engage in competition (iii) Grow about 1–3 inches a year
State True or False: (i) Preschoolers describe themselves mainly through concrete, observable features such as their name and possessions. (ii) Six-to-eight-year-olds are still egocentric.
questions.answer: (i) True. (ii) False — they are no longer egocentric and understand others' views.

questions.q: Answer in one word: (i) The cognitive limitation in which a child cannot see another person's point of view. (ii) The stage of cognitive development of three-to-six-year-olds.

sections.title: Very short answer questions. Answer in 30–50 words.

questions.q: How does the growth rate of children aged three to six years compare with that of infants?
questions.answer: Three-to-six-year-olds grow more slowly than infants but steadily — about 4–5 pounds and 2–3 inches a year — and need less sleep; their muscles and bones grow stronger and coordination improves.

questions.q: Write two examples each of gross motor and fine motor skills developed by children aged three to six years.
questions.answer: Gross motor: running, jumping, throwing and kicking; catching a bounced ball; pedalling a tricycle; hopping on one foot. Fine motor: drawing a circle or square; cutting with blunt scissors; buttoning clothes; tying shoelaces; using a spoon and fork.
questions.note: October 2024 asked for examples of gross motor skills only.

questions.q: What is a key aspect of preschoolers' socio-emotional development?
questions.answer: A growing self-concept: preschoolers describe themselves by concrete features — name, possessions, family, achievements ('I run fast'). They can talk about their feelings, complex emotions such as guilt, shame and pride appear, they learn social skills for playing with others, and they want to take initiative.

questions.q: What emerges during preschool age regarding gender identity?
questions.answer: Children classify themselves as male or female, prefer clothes and dressing suited to their own gender, use gender-typed language, and their play tends to reflect gendered practices.

questions.q: What is causality in preschool children's thinking?
questions.answer: The ability to think about the causes of familiar events, such as living things growing when they get food. But preschoolers cannot yet reason logically about cause and effect and may link two events that happen close together as cause and effect.
questions.note: October 2022 asked for a one-sentence explanation.

questions.q: What is symbolic function?
questions.answer: The preschooler's ability to keep an image of an object, person or event in mind and think about it without it being present, and to name it with symbols such as words and numbers.
questions.note: October 2022 asked for a one-sentence explanation.

questions.q: What is spatial thinking in preschoolers?
questions.answer: Understanding spatial relationships — for example, that a picture represents something not present but real — though preschoolers may not fully understand the relation between the picture and the actual object.
questions.note: April 2023 asked for a one-sentence explanation.

sections.title: Short answer questions. Answer in 50–80 words.

questions.q: Explain the different aspects of cognitive development of preschoolers.
questions.answer: Preschoolers are in Piaget's pre-operational stage. Symbolic function: they think of absent objects and use words and numbers as symbols. Spatial thinking: they understand that a picture stands for a real object. Causality: they think about causes of familiar events but may link events just because they happen together. Categorisation: they group objects as edible/inedible, friend/non-friend, but also show animism. Identities: they partly understand that objects stay the same when their form changes, but lack conservation. Egocentrism: they see only their own viewpoint (three-mountain task).

questions.q: List the abilities of a seven-year-old child in the cognitive, language and socio-emotional domains.
questions.answer: Cognitive: logical but concrete thinking, conservation of number, length, liquid and weight, reversibility, remembering routes, planning ahead, longer and selective attention, reading and writing. Language: sophisticated comprehension and use, clear speech to share opinions, turn-taking and sustained conversation, appreciation of humour, inventing words. Socio-emotional: realistic self-concept from strengths and weaknesses, verbalising conflicting emotions, wanting privacy, competitive games and teamwork with peers, developing sense of right and wrong.

questions.q: Describe the language development of preschool children.
questions.answer: Vocabulary expands rapidly and they use words easily in everyday talk; fast mapping helps them learn new words from context. They combine words into sentences and from three use plurals, possessives and past tense, and pronouns like I, me, you, we correctly. They become competent in pragmatics — knowing how to speak with whom, repeating or rephrasing when not understood. They can follow three-step commands, count to ten, name four colours, enjoy rhymes, answer 'why' questions and talk to themselves.

sections.title: Long answer questions. Answer in 80–120 words.

questions.q: What do you understand by play? Discuss the role of play in early childhood development.
questions.answer: Play is a child's freely chosen, joyful activity; Froebel called it a serious occupation, Montessori stressed free and spontaneous play, and Piaget defined it as responses repeated for functional pleasure. Role: it lays the foundation for literacy (new sounds and words), is itself learning, gives choice and lets children test their physical limits, and lets adults understand children's body language. Physical-motor: hopping, skipping and using writing tools build gross and fine skills, stamina and confidence. Socio-emotional: children control their play world, which builds self-esteem; they learn to cope with feelings, cooperate, negotiate roles and follow rules. Cognitive: counting, colours and problem solving. Language: internalising language rules and using language for different purposes, jokes and riddles. Aesthetic: creating and appreciating art.

questions.q: Make a comparative milestone chart of a three-year-old and a six-year-old child.
questions.answer: Physical-motor — three: runs, jumps, pedals a tricycle, scribbles, draws a circle, feeds self with a spoon; six: hops and balances on one foot, heel-to-toe walk, steers well, cuts a straight line with scissors, draws a triangle, dresses self, ties shoelaces. Socio-emotional — three: self-awareness, gender identity forming, plays beside or with a few peers, names basic feelings; six: describes self by abilities, plays cooperative games with rules, talks about feelings, shows guilt, shame and pride, takes initiative. Cognitive — three: symbolic thought, animism, egocentrism, no conservation; six: categorises, thinks about causes, beginning to overcome egocentrism, still pre-operational. Language — three: three-word sentences, plurals and past tense begin; six: long sentences, pragmatics, follows three-step commands, counts to ten, names colours, enjoys word play.
